notes.claim: The assignment has five boards (MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1, DBP2) and asks for a full design of the longest circuit from DBL2 and from DBP2, with relevant protective devices.

The project guide says to include all lengths of the cable run, calculations for thermal constraints, a comparison of Zs with the device's maximum, and the sum of all voltage drops from the intake equipment.
The formula sheet totals voltage drop as the submain's drop plus the final circuit's, and for a final circuit from a sub-board uses Zs = Zs@db + (R1+R2).
The showroom supply gives Ze 0.1 ohm, 4.6 kA prospective fault current and 20 degrees Celsius ambient; the motor and its cables are question 4.

Table 4E4A in your copy (p.464) gives the current-carrying capacity of multicore armoured 90 °C thermosetting cables: for four-core 4 mm² 42 A clipped direct (Reference Method C) and 44 A on a perforated tray in free air (Method E), three-phase; 1.5 mm² 23 A and 25 A; 2.5 mm² 31 A and 33 A.
Table 4E4B in your copy (p.465), three- or four-core three-phase column: 27 mV/A/m for 1.5 mm², 16 for 2.5 mm² and 10 for 4 mm²; the same table gives 31, 19 and 12 for two-core single-phase.

Table 41.3 maximum Zs for 0.4 s: type C 3.64 ohm at 6 A and 2.19 ohm at 10 A (a trade app printing the table; the pages are not among those saved from your copy). Type C suits high inrush loads including discharge lighting but leaves less Zs margin, so it should be chosen only where the load needs it.

LED drivers contain capacitors and draw an inrush current at switch-on that can trip a circuit-breaker; BEAMA and ABB set out how the breaker type and the driver datasheet decide how many drivers one breaker can carry.

Table 54.4 gives k for steel armour as 51 (70 °C thermoplastic) and 46 (90 °C thermoplastic or thermosetting) in a Certsure pocket guide; armour used as a cpc is thermally stressed in a fault, and the Zs must include the armour, glands and terminations. Read the real k from Table 54.4 in your copy: the lesson keeps it as a practice value.

The Electrical Installation Design Guide limits the Zs at the end of the circuit to the maximum values of Tables 41.2 to 41.4, and the Zs of a circuit from a sub-board is built from the Zs at the board plus the circuit's own R1+R2 (your formula sheet, step 13).

Where along a cable the thermal worst case lies is argued on the IET forum: shock protection is worst at the remote end, but the adiabatic check is not, so the fault current near the origin of the cable is the one that sets the cpc size. Taught as contested; Dan's own course checks the end of the cable being sized.

The tabulated three-phase mV/A/m values already contain the root 3 and assume balanced loads; for an unbalanced load one trade source says to work phase by phase with the single-phase values (a different route from your formula sheet, which divides the three-phase drop by root 3), taught as two routes; and the rating of a three-phase four-core cable assumes three loaded conductors.

Whether the design current of a lighting circuit is the connected load or the breaker's rating, with room left for later luminaires, is argued on the IET forum; the course sizes on its calculated figures and says so.
Both of Dan's drawings are 1:50 at A1 with no printed dimensions, so every length scaled from them is approximate.

Lighting must not drop more than 3% of the supply voltage (6.9 V single-phase, 12 V three-phase); the limit runs from the origin to the most distant point, and the submain's drop is added to the final circuit's (a three-phase drop is divided by root 3 to join a single-phase one).
Regulation 714.411.3.4: lighting the public can reach needs additional protection by a 30 mA RCD unless it is supplied from SELV; A4 adds that lighting includes its wiring and control gear.
A4's note to Regulation 522.8.10: an underground conduit with impact rating N750 counts as protection equal to armour for a buried cable.
Table 41.3 gives the overcurrent part of an RCBO to BS EN 61009-1 the same maximum Zs as the circuit-breaker of the same type and rating.

Under A4's Regulation 536.4.202 a board is protected against overload in one of three ways: the device feeding it is rated no higher than the board and any outgoing unit; load curtailment limits its demand; or its whole connected load without diversity fits. Diversity is never a means of overload protection.
